nodes.title: Security fundamentals: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Security is about layering defenses so no single failure compromises a system. Most exams test the same core ideas: least privilege, defense in depth, the CIA triad, and the shared-responsibility line between you and your cloud provider.

flashcards.front: What is the CIA triad?
flashcards.back: Confidentiality (only the right people see the data), Integrity (data isn't tampered with), Availability (the system is reachable when needed). Every security control maps to at least one of these three pillars.

flashcards.front: What does 'least privilege' mean?
flashcards.back: Grant each identity (user, role, service account) the minimum permissions needed to do its job — no more. The opposite is wildcard access, which makes a single credential leak catastrophic.

flashcards.front: What is defense in depth?
flashcards.back: Stack multiple, independent controls so an attacker has to defeat all of them. Example: WAF in front of an app, network ACL on the subnet, IAM on the workload, encryption at rest in the database.

flashcards.front: Shared responsibility model — who does what?
flashcards.back: The cloud provider secures the cloud (physical hardware, hypervisor, region facilities). You secure what's IN the cloud (your data, IAM config, OS patching on EC2, application code). The exact line shifts by service: serverless is more on the provider, IaaS is more on you.

nodes.title: Networking fundamentals: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Networking moves packets between machines using layered protocols (the OSI / TCP-IP stack). Most exam questions test routing decisions, subnetting math, the difference between L2 and L3, and how DNS / DHCP make the whole thing usable for humans.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between Layer 2 and Layer 3?
flashcards.back: L2 (data link) uses MAC addresses to deliver frames inside a single broadcast domain (a switch). L3 (network) uses IP addresses to route packets between networks (a router). Switches do L2; routers do L3.

flashcards.front: How does a subnet mask work?
flashcards.back: The mask splits an IP into a network portion (the high bits, set to 1) and a host portion (the low bits, set to 0). `/24` means the first 24 bits are network = up to 256 hosts (254 usable). `/30` is 4 IPs = 2 hosts — typical for a point-to-point link.

flashcards.front: What does DNS do?
flashcards.back: Domain Name System translates human-readable names (`example.com`) into IP addresses. A recursive resolver asks the root, the TLD server (`.com`), and finally the authoritative server for the domain. TTL controls how long answers are cached.

flashcards.front: TCP vs UDP — when do you pick each?
flashcards.back: TCP is reliable, ordered, congestion-controlled — use it when every byte matters (HTTP, SSH, SMTP). UDP is lightweight, no handshake, no retransmit — use it for streaming, gaming, DNS queries, anywhere latency beats reliability.

nodes.title: Cloud fundamentals (CLF-C02 / AZ-900 / CCNA): Key Ideas
nodes.content: Cloud fundamentals questions appear on almost every entry-level certification. They test your ability to map a business requirement to the correct service model (IaaS/PaaS/SaaS), understand the provider vs customer responsibility split, and compare on-premises capex to cloud opex — all before any technical deep-dive.

flashcards.front: IaaS vs PaaS vs SaaS — who manages what in each model?
flashcards.back: IaaS (EC2, Azure VM, Compute Engine): provider manages hardware + hypervisor; you manage OS, runtime, app, data. PaaS (App Service, Elastic Beanstalk, App Engine): provider adds OS + runtime; you manage app + data. SaaS (Office 365, Salesforce): provider manages everything; you manage user config and data. As you move up the stack you trade control for speed.

flashcards.front: Shared responsibility model — where is the exact dividing line?
flashcards.back: The provider is always responsible for security OF the cloud (physical data centers, networking fabric, hypervisor, managed service software). The customer is always responsible for security IN the cloud (data classification, IAM configuration, OS patching on IaaS VMs, application code). The dividing line shifts up the stack for PaaS and SaaS — the more managed the service, the more the provider owns.

flashcards.front: Regions vs Availability Zones — what is each?
flashcards.back: A region is a geographic cluster of data centers (e.g., us-east-1, West Europe). An AZ is one or more discrete data centers within a region with independent power, cooling, and networking. AZs in a region are close enough for low-latency synchronous replication but far enough apart that a fire/flood in one doesn't hit another. Spread workloads across at least 2 AZs for high availability.

flashcards.front: Capex vs opex — why does cloud shift the spending model?
flashcards.back: Capex (capital expenditure): large upfront purchase of hardware that you then depreciate over years; on-premises servers. Opex (operating expenditure): ongoing pay-as-you-go cost; cloud compute bills. Cloud converts infra from capex to opex — no hardware procurement lead times, costs scale with actual usage, easier to budget for a startup or to kill a failed project without a sunk-cost legacy.

nodes.title: Storage concepts: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Cloud storage comes in three flavors with very different cost/perf trade-offs: object (think S3), block (think EBS / managed disks), and file (think EFS / Azure Files / Filestore). Pick wrong and you either overpay or hit performance ceilings.

flashcards.front: Object vs block vs file storage — when do you use each?
flashcards.back: Object (S3, Blob, GCS) for unstructured data, backups, static sites, data lakes — flat namespace, HTTP API, infinite scale. Block (EBS, managed disks) for OS disks and databases — low latency, single attach. File (EFS, NFS) when multiple VMs need a shared POSIX filesystem.

flashcards.front: What is a storage class / tier?
flashcards.back: Same data, different SLA and price. Hot tier (frequent access, expensive read, cheap retrieval). Cold/archive tier (rare access, cheap to store, expensive to read, retrieval latency from minutes to hours). Lifecycle policies move data between tiers automatically.

flashcards.front: Why use server-side encryption?
flashcards.back: Data is encrypted at rest by the storage service using either provider-managed keys (default, no extra config) or your own keys via KMS. This protects against physical disk theft and meets compliance baselines without changing your app code.

flashcards.front: What's storage durability vs availability?
flashcards.back: Durability is the chance your data won't be lost (object stores claim ~11 9s — 99.999999999%). Availability is the chance you can reach it right now (typically 4 9s — 99.99%). Durability is multi-region replication; availability is how many concurrent failures the service tolerates.

nodes.title: Compute services: Key Ideas
nodes.content: 'Compute' is everything that runs your code: VMs, containers, serverless functions, batch jobs. The exam wants you to pick the right shape — long-running stateful workload → VM, packaged app → container, event-driven short job → serverless.

flashcards.front: VM vs container vs serverless — pick a service for each.
flashcards.back: VM (EC2 / Compute Engine / Azure VM) when you need full OS control. Container (ECS, GKE, AKS, Cloud Run) when you've packaged an app and want orchestration. Serverless (Lambda, Functions, Cloud Functions) for short event-driven tasks, no infrastructure to manage.

flashcards.front: What is autoscaling?
flashcards.back: A service that adds/removes compute instances based on a signal (CPU, request rate, queue depth, custom metric). Scale-out is cheap; scale-in saves money. Target tracking is the simplest mode: 'keep average CPU at 60%'.

flashcards.front: Spot / preemptible / low-priority — what's the catch?
flashcards.back: Up to 90% off list price, but the cloud can yank the instance with 30 s – 2 min warning. Use for fault-tolerant batch jobs, CI runners, big-data clusters. Don't use for stateful databases or anything that needs to stay up.

flashcards.front: Reserved / committed-use vs on-demand pricing.
flashcards.back: On-demand: pay by the hour or second, no commitment. Reserved / committed: 1-3 year commitment, 30-60% discount, no flexibility. Pick reserved for steady baseline load, on-demand for spiky workloads.

nodes.title: Cloud governance: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Governance is the set of policies and guardrails that keep a cloud account safe and on-budget as it scales from one engineer to a hundred. Think tagging standards, budget alerts, organizational policies, and the multi-account strategy.

flashcards.front: Why use multiple accounts (an Organization) instead of one big account?
flashcards.back: Blast-radius isolation: a compromised prod account doesn't leak into dev. Billing clarity: per-team or per-environment cost reports. Quota independence: prod doesn't share API limits with sandbox. Service Control Policies (AWS) / management groups (Azure) enforce 'no one can disable CloudTrail' across the whole org.

flashcards.front: What is a Service Control Policy (SCP)?
flashcards.back: An AWS Organizations policy that sets the maximum permissions any IAM identity in a member account can have. Even if a user's IAM policy grants `s3:*`, an SCP denying `s3:DeleteBucket` overrides it. SCPs are guardrails, not grants — they only restrict.

flashcards.front: Tagging strategy — name three high-leverage tags.
flashcards.back: (1) Owner / team — who pays and who to page. (2) Environment (prod/staging/dev) — drives access controls and lifecycle. (3) Cost-center / project — for chargeback. Tags are free and infinitely valuable for cost allocation and automation; enforce them with policies.

flashcards.front: What is a landing zone?
flashcards.back: A pre-baked multi-account setup with security baselines: org with master + audit + log-archive + workload accounts, CloudTrail / Config enabled everywhere, SSO wired up, network templates ready. AWS Control Tower / Azure Landing Zones / GCP setup automate this so you start on a safe foundation, not bare cloud.

nodes.title: Mixed exam topics: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Some exam objectives don't fit neatly into a single domain — they span protocols, tools, or concepts covered briefly in multiple sections. These cards treat each item as a stand-alone fact, the way an exam question presents it: one concept, one answer.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a hub, a switch, and a router?
flashcards.back: Hub: Layer 1, repeats every frame to all ports — all devices share bandwidth, collisions guaranteed. Switch: Layer 2, forwards frames using a MAC address table to only the destination port — full duplex, no collisions, each port gets full bandwidth. Router: Layer 3, makes forwarding decisions based on IP address, connects different networks. Hub is legacy; switches dominate LAN; routers are at network edges.

flashcards.front: What is RAID 5 and how many drives can it tolerate losing?
flashcards.back: RAID 5 stripes data and parity across at least 3 drives. Any single drive failure can be recovered by reconstructing missing data from the remaining drives and parity. It cannot tolerate 2 simultaneous drive failures. Effective capacity = (N-1) × drive size. Read performance is excellent; write requires parity recalculation. RAID 6 tolerates 2 failures using double parity.

flashcards.front: What does a proxy server do, and how does a forward proxy differ from a reverse proxy?
flashcards.back: Forward proxy: sits between clients and the internet on behalf of clients — used for content filtering, caching, and anonymizing outbound requests (the server sees the proxy's IP). Reverse proxy: sits in front of servers on behalf of the server — used for load balancing, SSL termination, caching, and hiding backend topology (the client sees the proxy's IP). Both intermediate HTTP, but they protect opposite sides.

flashcards.front: What is the purpose of a DMZ in network architecture?
flashcards.back: A demilitarized zone is a network segment between the untrusted internet and the trusted internal network, typically protected by two firewalls (or two interfaces on one firewall). Public-facing services (web, email, DNS) sit in the DMZ: internet can reach them but not the internal network; if the DMZ host is compromised, the inner firewall still blocks access to the internal LAN.
